edges.evidence: Both contributions directly address the quality of LLM-generated peer reviews relative to human reviews, but arrive at meaningfully incompatible conclusions. Contribution A finds that LLM-generated feedback overlaps with individual human peer reviews at rates comparable to the overlap between two human reviewers (e.g., ~30.85% vs. ~28.58% for Nature journals; ~39.23% vs. ~35.25% for ICLR), framing LLM feedback as substantially similar to human feedback in coverage (AQ, A:002, A:009). Contribution B, by contrast, conducts a sentence-level analysis and finds that LLM-generated reviews contain more deficient segments than human reviews, are paper-unspecific, lack diversity, and lack constructive feedback — explicitly quantifying a gap between LLM and human reviewing quality (BQ, B:002). Evidence B:009 further shows that inter-LLM BERTScore similarity (70.33–71.17) is notably higher than inter-human similarity (59.15), indicating LLMs produce less diverse reviews than humans, which directly conflicts with Contribution A's framing of LLM reviews as comparable to human reviews. The two contributions study the same construct (LLM vs. human review quality) and reach genuinely incompatible

Contribution A finds that LLM-generated reviews overlap with human reviews at rates comparable to inter-human overlap, implying LLMs can perform adequately as reviewers. Contribution B, while citing A's overlap finding, presents directly conflicting evidence: LLMs assign higher ratings to incomplete papers (title-only) than full papers and exhibit prestige bias in single-blind settings. These findings challenge A's positive framing by showing LLMs have inherent flaws that make them unreliable. The two contributions address the same construct (LLM suitability for peer review) and reach genuinely incompatible conclusions about LLM reliability and readiness.
